subject: general
question: What is the relationship between the radius of curvature and the focal length for spherical mirrors with small apertures?

options.text: Radius of curvature is equal to half the focal length
Radius of curvature is equal to thrice the focal length
Radius of curvature is equal to the focal length
Radius of curvature is equal to twice the focal length

solution:
The correct answer is __**Radius of curvature is equal to twice the focal length**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the study of optics, specifically for **spherical mirrors**, there is a fundamental geometric relationship between the **radius of curvature (R)** and the **focal length (f)**.
 
• The **radius of curvature (R)** is defined as the radius of the hollow sphere of glass of which the reflecting surface of the mirror forms a part. It is the distance from the **pole (P)** to the **center of curvature (C)**.
 
• The **focal length (f)** is the distance between the **pole (P)** and the **principal focus (F)** of the mirror.
 
• For **spherical mirrors** with a **small aperture**, the **principal focus (F)** lies exactly halfway between the **pole (P)** and the **center of curvature (C)**.
 
• This geometric arrangement leads to the mathematical formula: **R = 2f**. This implies that the **radius of curvature** is **twice** the **focal length**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Radius of curvature is equal to twice the focal length.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Spherical Mirrors**:
 
 
• **Concave Mirror**: A spherical mirror with its reflecting surface curved inwards, facing towards the **center of the sphere**. It is also known as a **converging mirror**.
 
• **Convex Mirror**: A spherical mirror with its reflecting surface curved outwards. It is also known as a **diverging mirror**.
 
 
 
• **Aperture**: The diameter of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is called its **aperture**. The relationship **R = 2f** is an approximation that holds true primarily for mirrors where the **aperture** is much smaller than the **radius of curvature**.
 
• **Principal Axis**: This is the imaginary straight line passing through the **pole** and the **center of curvature** of a spherical mirror.
 
• **Sign Convention**: According to the **New Cartesian Sign Convention**, the **focal length** of a **concave mirror** is considered **negative**, while the **focal length** of a **convex mirror** is considered **positive**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Paraxial Rays**: The derivation of the formula **R = 2f** assumes that the light rays are **paraxial**, meaning they strike the mirror very close to the **principal axis** and make small angles with it.
 
• **Spherical Aberration**: If the **aperture** of the mirror is large, the rays falling far from the axis (marginal rays) do not meet at the same **focal point** as the paraxial rays. This defect is known as **spherical aberration**.
 
• **Numerical Application**: If a **convex mirror** has a **radius of curvature** of **32 cm**, its **focal length** would be **16 cm** (f = R/2). Similarly, if a **concave mirror** has a **focal length** of **10 cm**, its **radius of curvature** is **20 cm**.
 
• This relationship is essential for using the **Mirror Formula**: **1/f = 1/v + 1/u**, where **v** is the image distance and **u** is the object distance.
